findings.evidence: "The branch managers' working group audits renewal rates on the first of every month... The consortium's circulation team reviews monthly checkout volume after each fiscal period."
findings.fix: Either remove this section or replace it with data that is actually used later (e.g., return-rate or fine-revenue tracking methodology), and explain how it connects to the recommendation.
findings.violation: This section introduces renewal-rate and checkout-volume tracking as background, but neither metric is used anywhere else in the document - the actual case rests entirely on return rates and a patron survey, so this section provides no support for the recommendation.

findings.evidence: "self-reported avoidance... dropped from 22 percent of respondents before the pilot to 5 percent after it... The survey was administered at the same pilot branches immediately before and twelve months into the pilot."
findings.fix: Either report the survey as a 12-month interim measurement rather than a post-pilot result, or explain why the 12-month mark is an appropriate proxy for the full 16-month pilot.
findings.location: ## What the Pilot Showed, second paragraph
findings.violation: The pilot ran 16 months, but the "after" survey was taken at month 12 - four months before the pilot ended - so calling it a before/after-the-pilot comparison overstates what was actually measured.

findings.evidence: "replacing the current fine notices with automatic email reminders sent three, seven, and fourteen days after the due date"
findings.fix: Either cite pilot data showing this specific reminder cadence was used and effective, or label the reminder schedule as a new, untested design choice rather than an evidence-backed outcome.
findings.violation: This specific reminder schedule is presented as part of the validated recommendation, but nothing in the pilot description mentions this reminder system being tested; the 94%/87% return-rate comparison cannot be attributed to a notice schedule that was never evaluated.

findings.evidence: "This recommendation applies to items returned within 60 days of their due date... matching the return-rate pattern the pilot data actually established."
findings.fix: Either present the specific pilot data (e.g., return-by-day distribution) that justifies the 60-day cutoff, or remove the claim that this threshold matches the pilot's established pattern.
findings.violation: No figure given earlier describes a 60-day window; the pilot data reported only an aggregate "on-time-or-eventual" return rate (94% vs. 87%), so claiming the 60-day cutoff "matches" a pattern the pilot "actually established" is unsupported by anything stated in the document.

findings.evidence: "...which is the reason the pilot's return-rate and avoidance-survey results, taken together, support ending fines for the whole consortium rather than only the pilot branches."
findings.fix: Replace the circular claim with an actual comparison showing the five non-pilot branches are similar enough to the pilot branches that the result should transfer, or acknowledge the uncertainty.
findings.location: ## Why the Pilot Result Applies Systemwide, first paragraph
findings.violation: This is circular reasoning - it asserts the generalization is justified because removing penalties "predictably" increases returns, using that predicted mechanism as proof the mechanism applies consortium-wide, without addressing whether the non-pilot branches resemble the pilot branches (size, demographics, usage patterns).

findings.evidence: "This relationship is documented in the Tri-County Library Data Cooperative's 2023 fines-elimination research brief, which reviewed return-rate data from fourteen library systems..."
findings.fix: Add a sentence establishing comparability (e.g., similar branch counts, patron demographics, or urban/rural mix) or drop the citation if comparability can't be shown.
findings.location: ## Why the Pilot Result Applies Systemwide, second paragraph
findings.violation: The document never establishes that the Tri-County cooperative's fourteen systems are comparable to this ten-branch consortium in size, patron base, or item mix, so the citation is used to support generalization without demonstrating relevance.

findings.evidence: "the four pilot branches absorbed the loss without a measurable change to their replacement-copy spending" compared with "## What the Pilot Showed": "During a 16-month pilot at 5 branches"
findings.fix: Correct one of the two figures so the branch count is consistent throughout the document.
findings.location: ## Addressing the Revenue Concern, second paragraph
findings.violation: The pilot is described as covering 5 branches earlier but as "four pilot branches" here - a direct numerical inconsistency about how many branches participated.
